corrections.claimed_speedup: BENCHMARKS.md 'Speed in context' (Big Buck Bunny, 10 s, 30.7 MB): Pare 24.9 s from the click, including the size plan and Auto's test encodes (13.4 MB, VMAF NEG 93.1, worst frame 88.9), vs ffmpeg.wasm 0.12 single-threaded x264 `faster` CRF 19 158.9 s and multithreaded 42.4 s (both 12.2 MB, VMAF NEG 93.0, worst frame 89.8): 6.4x and 1.7x as fast per the page; native ffmpeg x264 with Pare's settings 6.4 s. Pare's encode alone took 12.9 s, about twice native x264 on the same cores. README/RESEARCH.md: about 1,500 lines of WebAssembly SIMD128 kernels make encoding 2.0-2.3x faster per core than the plain C build with byte-identical output, and the single-thread WebAssembly build runs at 54% of native x264 with the same settings (4.25 vs 7.85 fps on park).
corrections.caveats: First-party and very new (94 commits, first in late September 2026, 3 stars). The headline 6.4x/1.7x over ffmpeg.wasm is a whole-pipeline comparison, not a kernel one: Pare adds chunked multi-worker encoding, WebCodecs decoding and its own x264 settings (diamond motion search and no 8x8-and-smaller inter partitions, about two thirds of the CPU time of the `faster`-based setting), while ffmpeg.wasm ran stock `faster` CRF 19; ffmpeg.wasm also produced a smaller file (12.2 MB vs 13.4 MB) at the same VMAF NEG with a better worst frame, and Pare's time includes finding its own rate factor. The cleanest kernel claim (2.0-2.3x per core over scalar C WebAssembly) is a sentence in RESEARCH.md without a per-kernel table. One run per row on a 4-core cloud VM shared with other work (the page reports up to 25 s variation between identical encodes in a busy session). Emscripten version unpinned. ffmpeg/ffmpeg is already catalogued; x264 itself was not in the known list.

notes: All claimed numbers appear verbatim in research/BENCHMARKS.md and README; repo metadata confirmed (GPL-2.0-or-later per README, LICENSE is GPL v2 text, 3 stars, 94 commits, latest commit 2026-09-28, not a fork). Main shortcoming: the ffmpeg.wasm gap mixes SIMD kernels with parallel chunking, browser decoding and cheaper encoder settings, and ffmpeg.wasm's output was 9% smaller at equal VMAF NEG; times come from a shared, noisy VM.

tier_reason: The repo is the artifact of the peer-reviewed paper 'Understanding the Performance of WebAssembly Applications', ACM Internet Measurement Conference (IMC) 2021, DOI 10.1145/3487552.3487827, first author Yutian Yan (venue confirmed from an OpenAlex record in a WebSearch result, snippet only; doi.org, dl.acm.org and api.openalex.org are blocked here). The README's RQ1 numbers match the claim; not A because the README states no CPU or device models and timings are read by hand from browser developer tools.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README RQ1: with extra-small and small inputs WebAssembly is faster than JavaScript in almost all benchmarks (97.6% and 95.1%), averaging 26.99x (extra-small) and 8.22x (small); with medium inputs 18 of 41 benchmarks become slower in WebAssembly (average slowdown 1.71x) and the remaining 23 average 6.70x faster. Example: 3mm is 47.71x, 10.54x and 1.12x faster in WebAssembly for extra-small, small and medium inputs. WebAssembly also uses 3.39-6.20x more memory than JavaScript across browsers.
corrections.caveats: A measurement study (IMC 2021 artifact) rather than a reusable library: the 'project' is Cheerp 2.0's WebAssembly output, and the JavaScript baseline is Cheerp's own JS output from the same C sources, not hand-written JS. Mixed outcome: the WebAssembly lead shrinks with input size and reverses for 18 of 41 benchmarks at medium inputs; WebAssembly uses 3.4-6.2x more memory. Browsers are from 2019-2020 (Chrome 79, Firefox 71, Edge 79), hardware is not stated in the README, and timings are copied manually from the browser console. Peer review confirmed only from a search-result snippet of the OpenAlex record (DOI 10.1145/3487552.3487827); the paper itself was not reachable. No license file, so reference only.
